1:
The first question is one of tense, and it rearranges the chapter. Ellicott renders it now the Lord had said and calls these three verses parenthetic, referring to a revelation made before the present interview began, needed to explain the confidence of Moses about the last plague. Clarke reports the same proposal from Calmet, since the verses that follow appear to have been spoken at the interview of the previous chapter; read both in the past tense and in a parenthesis, he says, the sense will be much more distinct than it now appears. Calvin agrees it is parenthetical and draws the consequence for the man rather than the text: it was not with self-conceived confidence that Moses was lately so elated, but because he had been forewarned that the contests were near their end, and he could not have interrupted his vocation unless he plainly knew he was arriving at its conclusion. Gill accepts the rendering and asks how far back it reaches, rejecting the suggestion that it goes as far as the appearance in Midian, which he calls too remote, and referring it to the last time Pharaoh sent for Moses.

The spoiling of the Egyptians produces the sharpest division, and it is about what needs defending. Henry justifies it as unpaid wages: this was the last day of their servitude and their masters would have sent them away empty, and though the patient Israelites were so fond of liberty that they would have been satisfied with that alone, he that executeth judgment for the oppressed would not let the labourers lose their hire. Calvin knows that argument and refuses it. Some allege the severe labours deserved a reward, so that God justly permitted a compensation of which they would otherwise have been defrauded; there is no necessity, he says, for these subtleties. The sole authority of God absolves them from the charge of theft, since his decree is above all laws and his will is their rule; what God has transferred to his own people must not be counted the property of others; and if the laws of war permit victors to gather the spoil, why less allowable for God, who had overcome the Egyptians in ten illustrious battles before compelling them to surrender? As to the pretense of borrowing, the women did not lie when they asked for vessels for sacrifice, since it lay with God afterwards to devote them to other uses. Keil states the mechanism without the apology, that Jehovah would make the Egyptians willing to give, and notes that the delivery of these instructions is not recorded here.

On the greatness of Moses two objections are raised. Ellicott feels the difficulty of supposing Moses wrote so of himself, since the man is not a title by which writers speak of themselves; but he finds it far more difficult to imagine anyone else giving him so bald and poor a designation, when to other writers he is a prophet, or a man of God, or the servant of the Lord, never simply the man. To the objection that very great does not comport with his meekness, he answers that it is a mere statement of fact necessary for understanding the narrative, since Moses had come to be regarded, by courtiers and Egyptians generally, as a personage almost on a par with the Pharaoh they revered as a god on earth. Clarke reads the same fact as protection: had Moses not appeared a person whom it would be dangerous to molest, violence would long since have been offered him. Calvin turns it into consolation: men's hearts are turned either way by God, who impelled the Egyptians to hate his people and could as easily incline them to give freely what they had harshly refused. Henry notices who did the respecting: though Pharaoh hated Moses, there were those of Pharaoh's servants who respected him.
4:
Who carries out the stroke is disputed, partly over whether it matters. Henry insists on the agent named in the text: Moses and Aaron were not ordered to summon this plague, since God says I will go out — and what is hell but to fall into the hands of the living God? Gill assumes a destroying angel inflicting a disease, very probably the pestilence on the authority of Josephus, but sudden and universal. Clarke reports that some have greatly magnified the question whether the ministry was of a good or an evil angel, and dismisses it: both are under God's jurisdiction, and though such destruction is supposed more proper for a bad angel, the works of God's justice are not less holy than the works of his mercy, so the highest archangel may with the utmost propriety be employed in either. Ellicott notes that Pharaoh, hardened as he is, is yet allowed a place for repentance: had he relented now, the death of the firstborn and the destruction in the Red Sea might both have been escaped. Calvin admires the courage rather than the message, since Moses willingly encounters the tyrant and boasts he shall be his conqueror; and Pharaoh must have been confounded with terror, since though so cruelly repulsed he dismissed the Prophet in safety.

On the hour and reach of the plague they agree, then diverge in what they notice. Ellicott observes that the particular night was not specified, so suspense was added to the pain of unintermittent fear, though the hour was placed beyond doubt and was the dreadest of the twenty-four. Henry presses it differently: they should not die silently and insensibly, so as not to be discovered till morning, but so as to rouse the families at midnight to stand by and see them die. He reads the sequence as evidence of God's slowness to wrath: the death of the firstborn was threatened first and executed last, and had the death of their cattle humbled them their children would have been spared. Ellicott adds philology and sociology: the Hebrew word applies only to males, so in every family the eldest son should be cut off, and in Egypt as elsewhere primogeniture prevailed, the firstborn of Pharaoh bearing a title that made him hereditary crown prince. Calvin notes the same range in reverse, the heir of the kingdom first among the victims and afterwards the humbler people, the maid-servants at the revolving mills occupying a very low and despised condition.

Two things are singled out for extended treatment. Clarke stops on the mill, describing the portable millstones still used in the east, the upper one turned by a lever fixed in the rim; he has before him a drawing of such a machine as used in China, where the grinder pushes the lever and runs round with the stone; and he quotes a traveller's observation that when the stone is large a second person is called in, the women seating themselves opposite each other with the stone between them — which explains both sitting behind the mill and the saying that two women shall be grinding at the mill. These mills, he adds, were used among our own ancestors under another name and survive in Shetland and Iceland. The extension to the beasts draws the other extended comment, and the two answers are opposed. Ellicott calls it very remarkable and connects it with the Egyptian animal-worship, since four animals were regarded as actual incarnations of deity, three of them bulls and one a white cow, and it is not unlikely all were required to be firstborn. Calvin forbids the question: why God postponed punishing the fathers, whose sin was greater, and why in wreaking vengeance on the beasts he spared men, it is not our province curiously to inquire, since it is sinful to prescribe to God the measure of his judgments.
7:
The dogs are read three ways. Ellicott disposes of the clause in a line, calling the expression evidently proverbial. Gill offers both senses and will not choose: taken literally it was extraordinary that no dog should sharpen his tongue when six hundred thousand men besides women and children set out through many places where dogs were; taken figuratively, no Egyptian however spiteful should hurt an Israelite. Clarke reports the proverbial reading, then hazards a conjecture that turns the verse into a counter-stroke against the Egyptian gods. Is the allusion not to the known custom of dogs howling where there is a mortality — which he attributes not to prescience but to the keenness of their scent? Dogs were sacred in Egypt and so preserved in multitudes, and one of the chief deities had a son worshipped as a dog, or a man with a dog's head — the barking Anubis, who had a temple in a city the Greeks called the city of the dog, whose worship Scripture may acknowledge only to show its nullity. So the great cry through all the land may be that very howling, while among the Israelites there was no death and no dog moved his tongue — the object of Egyptian worship deploring a calamity it could not prevent, and powerless against the worshippers of Jehovah.

The anger of Moses is the second thing they dwell on, and Calvin does the work. Moses, having reported the words of God, now speaks in his own person, and the asperity wounded the tyrant: it was as if he had said that thus far he had entreated leave to depart, but now, whether Pharaoh would or not, he would freely go, and not without Pharaoh's own request. On the heat of anger he holds that the servants of God, even when faithfully performing their duty, are so disturbed with indignation against sin that they are by no means restrained from anger, and that Moses was excited by the impulse of the Spirit, which awakened the zeal and at once moderated it; yet since we are prone to impetuous passions, the spirit of gentleness must be asked of God to prevent excess. He then turns on a kind of critic: the anger of Moses proves God would not have us perform our duties lazily, and nothing is more preposterous than for cynics who sting God's servants with wanton witticisms to deride a vehemence rather worthy of the highest praise. Henry finds the cause in disappointed expectation, Moses having looked for the threat itself to induce compliance, and reads the meekest of men as grieved for the hardness of a heart. Ellicott adds the scene predicted: the officers about Pharaoh would come and prostrate themselves before Moses as if he were their king.

The closing verses divide them on the hardening. Henry takes the failure as proof: Moses did all these wonders before Pharaoh, an eye-witness of them, and yet could not prevail, which was a certain sign that God himself had in righteous judgment hardened his heart. Clarke attacks the English that permits it. Shall and will are both signs of the future and used indiscriminately by many, but here they differ essentially: shall not hearken intimates that it was impossible and that God had placed him under the impossibility, whereas will not hearken agrees with the earlier passages where Pharaoh hardened his own heart, proving that he refused without impulsive necessity and that God took advantage of the obstinacy to multiply his wonders. Clarke then leaves the argument for the text, reporting that the Samaritan copies here are fuller and better connected: the eighth verse has no natural connection with the seventh in the received Hebrew, contrary to the custom of Moses, who always notes where his discourses begin; and across five chapters the Hebrew gives each of seven judgment-speeches once where the Samaritan gives it twice.
